# docs_audit_report — 2026-06-13

## TL;DR (stranger's 30-second take)
The hero is genuinely good — one clear sentence about what it does, a `pip install`
line, Apache 2.0 — but a numerate stranger bounces within 30 seconds because the page
argues with itself about its own headline number (six different AUROC/AUC figures, one
of them a nonsensical "0.125 baseline") and the very first card under the stats is a
visually-broken box full of insider jargon ("Repinned from v2 0.9857"). The Evidence
section reads as acronym soup, and the blog directly below it is a reel of "here's how
our own numbers got caught cheating / retracted." I'd click GitHub if I were charitable,
close the tab if I were skeptical.

## TOP 3 PROBLEMS
1. The AUROC zoo + a sub-random "baseline" — Evidence section + hero stats bar. Six
   competing figures (0.9131 / 0.8947 / 0.9857 / 0.91 / 0.90 / 0.125), "FoVer" used as
   both the win and a weak baseline, and several suspiciously-perfect scores destroy
   trust in every number on the page.
2. The hero's "Recent progress" card is broken AND jargon-laden — it is crammed inside
   the four-column stats flexbox (renders as a misaligned bordered box; there's even a
   stray `</div>`) and the first prose a stranger reads is "Repinned from v2 0.9857 ...
   architecture-only 0.8947 ... 5-seed dual-condition."
3. The blog section reads as a confession reel — "Caught Cheating," "Two Retractions
   and a Rescue," "Regex in an NTK Costume," "Why We Report Two AUROCs" sit right under
   the Evidence grid and tell a stranger the project's numbers repeatedly get
   fabricated/retracted.

## DETAILED FINDINGS

### Bloat
- Evidence section-desc (lines 511–515) — ~55 words of defensive hedging
  ("infrastructure, hardware, ensemble, synthetic-pilot, and adversarial-audit rows are
  labeled by provenance ... they are not model-generation headline claims"). A stranger
  doesn't need a fabrication-disclaimer above the results; it reads as pre-emptive
  self-defense and signals the opposite of confidence. Cut to one sentence.
- Hero "Recent progress" r-card (line 312) — ~47 words; under the 60-word cap, but for
  the FIRST card on the page it should be ~20 words of plain English, not a changelog
  entry. Suggested cap: 25 words, zero version numbers.
- Results grid — 12 cards is under the 20-card cap, but a stranger will skim none of
  them because every tag is an unfamiliar acronym (see jargon). Volume + opacity
  compound. Suggest 4–6 headline cards with plain-English tags.
- Nav — 11 text links + 2 buttons (lines 265–284). Choice overload; "Get Started" /
  "Tutorial" / "Quick Start" are three overlapping entry points, and "Report" / "Paper"
  / "Writing" are three more. Suggest ~5 links max.

### Internal jargon
- Hero "Recent progress" card (line 312) — "Repinned from v2 0.9857", "architecture-only
  0.8947", "5-seed dual-condition", "FoVer". A stranger has no idea what "repinned"
  means, why there was a previous "v2" number, or what "architecture-only" excludes.
  This is changelog narrative, not landing-page copy.
- Features card "Test-Time Compute (TTC) & PREM" (lines 497–499) — "Process-Reward
  Energy Model (PREM) variance", "intrinsic motivation for continuous self-learning."
  Highest jargon density on the page; near-unparseable to a non-insider. Expanding the
  acronyms inline doesn't help when the underlying concept is never explained.
- Features card "Research operations" (lines 469–477) — "adversarial-verify pass",
  "methodology-incomplete artifacts", "headline claims." This is internal dev-process,
  not a capability a user "checks" (and the section is titled "What you can check").
- Results tags — acronym soup with zero glosses: "SVAMP" (549), "VeriCoT ... CoT" (559),
  "CRANE" (554), "PRM-BiasBench" (564), "HalluGuard v3" (569), "CCTU" (451, 574),
  "GSM8K ... TP rate" (560), "Ising-guided fuzzing" (544). A stranger can't tell which
  are datasets, methods, or competitors.
- Preprint section (lines 584, 591–594) — "(paper-v6)" in the title, plus "non-operator
  environment" and "operator-initiated upload." "Operator" is internal terminology for
  the maintainer; a stranger reads it as oddly impersonal/robotic.
- "AUROC" / "AUC" used throughout with no one-line gloss for a non-ML reader (e.g. hero
  stat line 308). Borderline — acceptable for an ML audience, but the page otherwise
  pitches to a general "stranger at a conference."

### Per-milestone narrative
- Hero "Recent progress" card (line 312) — "Repinned from v2 0.9857 after pre-submission
  adversarial audit" is a status-update sentence lifted from internal process, not copy
  written for a reader.
- "HalluGuard v3" (line 569) and "(paper-v6)" (line 584) — bare internal version numbers
  surfaced on public cards; a stranger neither knows nor cares there were a v1/v2 or
  five prior paper drafts.

### Inconsistencies
- "FoVer" is the benchmark Carnot WINS on (line 308: "0.9131 Verifier AUROC — FoVer
  math step-errors") AND simultaneously a weak BASELINE it crushes (line 550: "0.90 AUC
  vs 0.125 FoVer baseline"). Same name, two contradictory roles. A stranger cannot tell
  whether FoVer is the test, a rival, or Carnot's own component.
- Headline number is not stable across the page: 0.9131 (line 308), 0.8947 (line 312),
  0.9857 (line 312, the retracted "v2"), 0.91 (line 530, prompt-injection), 0.90 (line
  550). The two ~0.91 figures (FoVer 0.9131 vs prompt-injection 0.91) are different
  things but round to the same value — a skimmer conflates them.
- Meter widths don't encode a consistent scale: "+3.0 points" → 14.6% bar (line 521)
  but "+4.9 points" → 66.7% bar (line 526). The bars imply +4.9 is ~4.5× bigger than
  +3.0; it isn't. Meanwhile the "4% → 12%" card (line 576) shows a near-empty 12% bar
  that visually reads as a failure.
- Problem section (line 338) shows the LLM "committed to '47 + 28 = 7'" while the intro
  and the other card say the wrong answer is "76" (lines 329, 343). The intermediate
  "= 7" looks like a third arithmetic typo stacked on the example; the point (mid-stream
  commitment) is lost on a fast reader.

### Missing essentials
- No single trustworthy headline number a stranger can walk away repeating. "What's THE
  result?" has six candidate answers and no clear winner.
- "Why should I trust the numbers?" is actively undermined: the Evidence desc pre-defends
  against fabrication, the cards show implausibly perfect scores, and the blog advertises
  repeated self-caught cheating/retractions. (What it DOES does, install, license, and
  maintainer are all present — those essentials are fine.)
- "Preprint" with a "Read paper" button that is a self-hosted PDF, not an arXiv listing
  ("arXiv submission is prepared but pending ... upload," line 593). Calling it a
  preprint when it isn't posted is a small credibility liability for a careful stranger.

### Fabrication signals
- "GSM8K extraction TP rate: 0.5 → 1.0" (line 560) — a perfect 1.0 true-positive rate
  with no sample size or anchor. Reads as too-clean.
- "k=5 ensemble catches 60/60 attacks" (line 565) — 100% catch rate, no false-positive
  rate shown. 60/60 is at least a concrete denominator, but a perfect score with no FPR
  context invites suspicion.
- "0.90 AUC (vs 0.125 FoVer baseline)" (line 550) — an AUC of 0.125 is FAR below random
  (0.5); a real classifier scoring 0.125 would simply be inverted to 0.875. A "baseline"
  this bad looks either mislabeled or chosen to flatter the 0.90. Biggest single
  credibility flag on the page.
- Two result meters pinned to 100% with perfect/round claims ("identical losses" 2.0×,
  line 540; "Ising sampler live on silicon," line 535) — individually defensible, but in
  aggregate with the above they reinforce a too-perfect impression.

## WHAT'S WORKING
- The hero nails the one-sentence pitch: "checks whether an answer is internally
  consistent — and suggests a fix when it isn't," with `pip install carnot-ebm` and the
  Apache 2.0 badge right there. A stranger immediately knows what it is and that it's
  free/open.
- The "How it works: Extract → Check → Repair" section and the 47+28 worked example are
  concrete, jargon-light, and genuinely explain the idea to a non-specialist. The Quick
  Start code block is clean and credible.
